source.title: Don't Forget It! Conditional Sparse Autoencoder Clamping Works for Unlearning
source.authors: Matthew Khoriaty; A. Shportko; G. Mercier; Zach Wood-Doughty

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests forgetting and recovery under an adversarial suffix attack using SAE clamping and RMU, but does not reproduce the recovery attacks or methods in the claim as a whole.
record.gate_note: The paper reports WMDP-Bio and MMLU accuracy for the unmodified model, RMU, Clamp Prime, and Refusal-clamp, plus a Concurrent Greedy Search suffix-attack evaluation for the base model, RMU, and Refusal-clamp. Feature frequencies and the top-k hyperparameter sweep are not separate results for the claim. The cited findings from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study builds a new SAE clamping method and an RMU comparator on gemma-2-2b. It reports WMDP-Bio forgetting and MMLU retention for each. It also reports a preliminary adversarial-suffix (prompt-only) recovery attempt on RMU and Refusal-clamp. Its own results therefore bear on A (unlearning works), E (prompt recovery) and F (a newer method claimed to resist attacks). It runs no fine-tuning, ablation or quantization recovery experiment.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors conclude that conditional SAE clamping beats prior SAE-based unlearning on retention. They say it brings WMDP-Bio accuracy near chance and performs comparably to RMU on forgetting and retention, with fewer hyperparameter choices. Refusal-clamp gets the best alignment score, at a noticeable MMLU cost. They call the adversarial test preliminary. They also say its failure even on RMU indicates the attack was too weak or ill-chosen. They note that SAE steering only protects closed-weight models, since the hooks are trivially removable.
record.recipe_differences: The main method is conditional SAE activation clamping rather than gradient ascent, Who's Harry Potter, or another recovery intervention in the claim. The paper also trains RMU models as a comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported results vary across RMU, Clamp Prime, and Refusal-clamp; the SAE methods show different MMLU retention scores.
record.code_released: The authors state that they plan to open-source the code after publication; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The adversarial evaluation uses one randomly sampled question-answer pair and one suffix-search setup. The authors state that more compute, more question-answer pairs, and a wider range of adversarial attacks are needed. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible separately reported results were left out.

untested.parts: Only one model (gemma-2-2b) and only WMDP-Bio (no Cyber or Chem). General ability is measured only on 4 MMLU subjects. Robustness is tested only against one suffix attack on one question. Clamp Prime was not attacked. There are no fine-tuning, ablation or quantization attacks.
Not tested: no relearning or fine-tuning experiment.
Not tested experimentally. The authors only note that steering hooks are trivially removable with weight access.
Only Concurrent Greedy Search suffixes on one sampled WMDP-Bio question. No rephrasing, jailbreak templates, other languages or in-context information.
Refusal-clamp is tested against only the one suffix attack. Not tested against fine-tuning, activation ablation, quantization, or removal of the inference-time hooks.

record.verdict_notes:
Changes from the earlier verdict:
(1) Merged the duplicate r10 items into one item (versions A and E, state absent). Merged the duplicate r11 items into one item (versions A, E and F, state absent). In each, the state describes the row's measure (recovery), and the problem text says how that bears on each version.
(2) Added a caveat to r10. The text says the attacked RMU model 'had the lowest accuracy on WMDP-Bio', but Table 1's RMU (0.3150) is the highest of the three unlearned models. The attacked RMU may therefore be a different model from the hyperparameter sweep than the one in r3/r4.
(3) Noted on r2 that the MMLU subject set is stated inconsistently: a footnote adds college biology to the four subjects in Section 3.
(4) Added one-model and Bio-only limits to untested A.
(5) Lightly extended authors_conclusion.
Judgments kept from the earlier verdict:
- Row versions V1/V5/V6 were relabelled by content to A/E/F. RMU rows do not get F, because RMU is the attacked original method.
- The E 'challenges' and F 'supports' labels rest on one question and one attack setup. Even on the base model, the attack produced only related text, not the target answer.
- The authors themselves argue the null attack result is weak, citing Tamirisa et al. on RMU being breakable with more compute.
- The authors state that SAE steering hooks are trivially removed by anyone with the weights. That is an argument, not a measured result, but it bears on C and F: the method blocks access at inference rather than deleting knowledge.
- The authors say MMLU retention may be inflated for biology-adjacent subjects.
- No uncertainty is reported.
- No instructions to the reader were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Tests RMU and SAE clamping on WMDP-Bio and MMLU, and suffix-attack recovery for RMU and Refusal-clamp. Does not test other unlearning methods or broader definitions of general ability.
No fine-tuning or relearning-set recovery experiment.
No activation-direction ablation recovery experiment or analysis establishing that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Tests only Concurrent Greedy Search adversarial suffixes on one sampled question-answer pair. Does not test ordinary rephrasing, other languages, or in-context information.
Tests Refusal-clamp against one suffix-search attack and compares it with RMU. Does not test resistance to fine-tuning, activation ablation, quantization, or other prompting attacks.

tranche.reason: A different method (conditional SAE clamping) on the same question, with an RMU comparator, a forgetting/retention evaluation and a suffix attack.

source_check.notes: The adversarial test is one question with one 32-token suffix (200 iters); the authors blame the RMU result on too weak an attack. SAE clamping leaves the weights unchanged, and the authors say the hooks are trivial to remove with weight access (closed weights only). MMLU is a 4-subject subset. The attacked RMU is described as the lowest-WMDP-Bio RMU model, so it may not be the Table 1 checkpoint.

statements.correction: gemma-2-2b (2B, pre-trained), WMDP-Bio (fractions): 0.5860->0.2985 (Clamp Prime, top-5, c=-300) and 0.2718 (Refusal-clamp, top-10, c=-500, t=0.05). 4-subject MMLU: 0.5710->0.5517 and 0.5352. Refusal-clamp still output gibberish under one Concurrent Greedy Search suffix (32 tokens, 200 iters) on one WMDP-Bio question. Preprint. SAE clamping is an inference-time hook; the authors say anyone with the weights can trivially remove it.
statements.problem: Cites r5 and r7 but states no fact about this study. Its conditions are wrong for this study: '6–70B' (gemma-2-2b is 2B) and 'No recovery attack on these checkpoints' (Refusal-clamp, r7, was suffix-attacked). 'All four report their own proposed methods' leaves this fifth study out. The forgetting-side citation itself is right.

What it says about this study is right: RMU kept outputting gibberish under the suffix attack (Sec. 5.1). Caveats: one sampled question only, and the attacked RMU is described as the lowest-WMDP-Bio RMU model.

statements.correction: Optional addition: gemma-2-2b RMU and Refusal-clamp; Concurrent Greedy Search suffix (32 tokens, b=32, k=64, t=200) on one WMDP-Bio question. Both kept outputting gibberish; the attack steered the base model to E. coli/viral RNA text. The authors call this preliminary and blame the RMU failure on an attack that was too weak.
statements.problem: Nothing it says is wrong, and the headline (GCG-family suffixes fail in some settings) fits this study. But the study is cited (r9-r11) without being described in 'what' or 'conditions'.
